name: Screen time and device overuse
seo_title: How Much Screen Time for Kids? UK Guide (2026)
seo_description: How much screen time is too much? The UK's 2026 guidance for under-5s, signs of overuse in older children, and practical ways to find a balance at home.
h1: Screen time and device overuse: a guide for parents
lead: Screens are part of family life, and a lot of what children do on them is good. The worry is when screens push out sleep, play, school and people. Here's what the UK guidance says and what helps.
answer_question: How much screen time is OK for children?
answer: For under-5s, the UK government's 2026 guidance says avoid screens for under-2s apart from shared moments like video calls, and keep 2 to 5-year-olds to about an hour a day. For older children there's no official number: what matters is whether screens are crowding out sleep, activity and family time.

sections.heading: The UK guidance for under-5s
body: In March 2026 the government published its first screen time guidance for parents of under-5s, on the Best Start in Life website.
list: Under 2: avoid screens, except shared activities such as video calls with family
2 to 5: try to keep it to 1 hour a day, less if possible
Choose slow, simple programmes over fast, social media-style videos
No social media, and no AI toys, tools or chatbots for young children
No screens in the hour before bed, and keep bedrooms and mealtimes screen-free

sections.heading: Older children and teens
body: There's no official daily limit for over-5s. In January 2026 the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, representing 23 UK medical bodies, warned of a "public health emergency" from children's unrestricted use of devices and social media. Ofcom found 8 to 14-year-olds spend the equivalent of one day a week online, and 15 to 17-year-olds two days.

subsections.heading: Sleep
body: Phones in bedrooms mean late-night scrolling, notifications and tired children the next day.

subsections.heading: Mood
body: Irritability, meltdowns when asked to stop, and low mood after long sessions.

subsections.heading: Body
body: Less time moving, and aches from hunching over a phone.

subsections.heading: Everything else
body: Homework, hobbies, friends and family time get squeezed out.

sections.heading: Finding a balance
list: Look at their screen time together, without judgement
Agree times and places: no phones at meals or in bedrooms overnight
Use time limits by app category, set from your own phone
Plan things to do offline, and allow them to be bored
Lead by example: your habits shape theirs
after: On iPhone, use Time Allowances and Screen Time Schedule. On Android, use Google Family Link. YouTube and TikTok have their own limits too.

sections.heading: Signs it's become a problem
list: Big reactions when asked to stop
Tiredness, or using devices late at night in secret
Losing interest in things they used to love
Falling behind at school, or pulling away from family and friends

sections.heading: What I'd do as a parent
body: Make the rules together and write them down, so they're about the family, not a punishment. Phones charge downstairs overnight, for everyone. And notice what they're doing on screens, not just how long: an hour making music is different from an hour of scrolling.
list: "What do you enjoy most on your phone?"
"How do you feel after a long scroll?"
"What would be a fair rule for all of us, me included?"

teachers: Tiredness in class is often a late-night phone problem. Encourage parents to keep devices out of bedrooms overnight, and point families of under-5s to the government's Best Start in Life screen time guidance.

faq.q: How much screen time should a 2-year-old have?
faq.a: UK guidance says try to keep 2 to 5-year-olds to 1 hour a day, less if possible, and avoid screens for under-2s except shared moments like video calls.

faq.q: How much screen time is too much for a teenager?
faq.a: There's no official UK limit for teens. Watch whether screens are affecting sleep, mood, schoolwork and time with family and friends.

faq.q: Should my child have their phone in their bedroom at night?
faq.a: It's best not to. Charging phones outside bedrooms overnight helps sleep for children and adults alike.

faq.q: How do I set screen time limits?
faq.a: Use your child's device controls: Time Allowances on iPhone or Google Family Link on Android. Many apps have their own limits too.

help: Worried about your child's wellbeing? Childline is free and confidential on [0800 1111](tel:08001111), any time. You are not alone.
sources: Best Start in Life (DfE and DHSC), screen time guidance for under-5s, 27 March 2026
Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, letter to government, reported January 2026
Ofcom, "Younger phone owners, the rise of AI, and consumption over creation", 21 May 2026
